Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 112, verses 1–4:

Say, "He is Allah, the One" (112:1). The word "Ahad" is deeper than "Wahid," because Ahad adds to the meaning of Wahid that nothing else truly exists alongside Him, and there is nothing like Him; that is, He is unique.

In "Ahad" there is an expression of the oneness of existence (wujud): that is, there is no reality other than His reality, and there is no true existence other than His. All existent things other than Allah derive their existence from Allah and take their reality from His reality. He is also One in agency (fa'iliyyah), so in this whole universe there is no other effective cause and no other agent besides Allah. Therefore, this is a doctrine and belief that settles in the conscience of a human being, and it is in fact also the interpretation of this universe. When this belief takes root in a heart, and reason conceives of it, and the whole universe is interpreted in its light, then no other conception overshadows the human heart, and no other thought remains even a trace in the human heart. The human heart then has no connection with anyone except that One Being, the Necessary Existent, because in truth the One Being alone truly exists, and it is this One Being alone who acts and causes effect.

Then the connection of the human heart with all the things found in this universe comes to an end. Although the ideal would be that awareness of the existence of anything other than Allah itself disappears from the human heart, even if this awareness does not disappear, the connection ends, because apart from the existence of Allah, the existence of all other things has no reality. And in this whole universe, nothing other than the agency and influence of Allah's will is active and effective. So why should the heart of one who holds the belief of Tawhid be attached to something that neither truly exists nor is active and effective in anything?

Now, when the heart becomes empty of the conception of the reality of all things other than the One God, and has no connection with anything other than Allah, then this heart truly becomes free; it becomes free of every kind of restriction. All its desires end, and the truth is that desires are in fact the chains on the feet. Then fear also departs from this heart, and it should be remembered that a person is also bound in chains because of fear. Why do the enjoyable things of the world end in the heart of a person? Because when he attains Allah, he attains everything, and he does not fear because he comes to know that there is no effective agent other than Allah.

When the reality settles firmly in human consciousness that in this universe a person sees only the reality of Allah, the result is that whatever existence he then sees in this universe, he will see the same reality in it. In this way, the human heart sees the hand of power (dast-e-qudrat) in everything, and after this, a person reaches the rank where he sees nothing in this universe except Allah.

As a result of this belief and conception, a person begins to think that apparent causes are also insignificant. The real and true cause is the Causer of causes, that is, the Divine Being. This is the point to which the Qur'an has given much attention, and it has sought to place it in the minds of people by making it part of the articles of faith of Islam. Accordingly, by setting aside apparent causes, it has been explained that the real cause is the Divine Will.

"And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw" (8:17). And in Al-Imran (3:126) it was said: "Victory is only from Allah." And in Al-Insan (76:30): "And you do not will except that Allah wills." There are countless verses of this kind.

When a person sets aside apparent causes, then he sees that all matters are determined by the will of Allah. From this, tranquility arises in his heart; now he seeks all desirable things from Allah and seeks refuge with Allah to protect himself from all undesirable things, and the apparent factors, apparent causes and influences which appear to act in this universe have no reality in his eyes.

These are the stations which the Sufis have sought to traverse. But the attraction of these stations took them far away. The Sufis could not understand that Islam, by calling people, certainly takes them to these lofty stations, but it takes them there while keeping them within all the ups and downs of practical worldly life, within every kind of human life, and while performing the duties of vicegerency (niyabat) of Allah on this earth. They participate fully in the life of this world and also consider it insignificant. They live in this universe, but they regard only Allah as the truly existent. They regard Allah as the one who is active and effective in all events and occurrences. And Islam adopts no other method than this, nor does it desire any other. As a result, a complete system of life comes into being. This system has come into being as a result of this interpretation of the universe and the consciousness, conceptions and tendencies arising from it. What are the features of this system of life?

(1) This system has its own system of worship in which only Allah is worshipped, the Allah whose existence has no reality apart from His existence, whose agency has no other agency besides it, and no other will is effective besides His will.

(2) This is a system in which a person turns in every state, in hope and in fear, only to Allah. In joy and in sorrow, in wealth and in poverty, in short, in every state his direction is only towards Allah alone. This is because in this system every person knows that when no other thing has real existence apart from Allah, then what is the benefit of turning to or calling upon it? When there is no agent or effective cause other than Allah, then what would be gained by turning towards anything else?

(3) This is a system in which guidance is taken only from Allah. Beliefs and doctrines, values and standards, Shari'ah and law, institutions and administration, customs and traditions, manners and conventions, all are derived from Allah. Therefore, every kind of guidance and direction is taken only from Allah alone, who is the One Existent both in reality and in the conscience of a Muslim.

(4) This system is a system of movement and action, and this movement and action is solely for Allah alone: for seeking His pleasure, for seeking His nearness, in the hope that on the path to reaching Him all veils and obstacles will be removed, and a person will be protected from all the impurities of misguidance, whether these veils and obstacles are within the human self, or come from the things and people of the human environment, among which the self of a person, the fear of people, his desires, and the things he loves in this world are foremost.

(5) This is a system which, alongside the above matters, creates a relationship of love, affection, cooperation and harmony between the human heart and all the existents of this universe. This is because freedom from the bonds of the world does not mean that a person regards it as detestable, hates it, flees from it, and refrains from using it. This is because all the things of the world are the wonders of Allah's power. Their existence is derived from the existence of Allah, and upon all things the light of that reality falls. Therefore all these things are beloved, because they are gifts of Allah, who is the Beloved.

(6) This is an exceptionally lofty and free system. In its eyes the earth is a small ball, the goods of the world are worthless, and freedom from these veils and obstacles is everyone's desire. But freedom from the slavery of the world does not mean that a person should become detached from worldly affairs and leave this world aimless, or hate it and flee from it. Rather, the demand of the Islamic system is continuous struggle, lasting effort, that humanity be advanced to ever higher levels, and that human life be fully free and liberated. Thus one aspect of worldly life is that it is the office of divine vicegerency, which has its own responsibilities, but in discharging these responsibilities, a person is neither a slave to them nor free of them, as we have explained.

There is one way of escaping the world which the churches prescribed, but Islam does not subscribe to monastic renunciation, because a human being has to perform the duties of earthly vicegerency, and people need good leadership. These two matters are necessary for human salvation, deliverance, and freedom from the slavery of this world. This path is very difficult; that is, the realization of human humanity is possible only in this manner. In this way, spirituality comes to dominate the personality of a human being, and this is freedom: the human soul, freed from worldly defilements, returns freely to its original source, and while working in the world in which Allah has placed a human being after creating him, he maintains his lofty spiritual station and reality.

This is why, at the beginning of the prophetic mission, the call was restricted solely to the belief of Tawhid, and in the above sense an attempt was made to establish the belief of Tawhid in people's minds, because in this sense Tawhid is a belief settled in the human heart and conscience, it is also an interpretation, explanation and understanding of this universe, and it is also a complete system of life. In this meaning, the belief of Tawhid is not merely words which are affirmed by the tongue, nor merely a firm conviction of the human conscience and consciousness which remains hidden only within conscience and consciousness. It is all of this, it is the whole religion; rather, it is the details of this belief. It has certain consequences, and these details and consequences are the natural and necessary results of this belief, and these results appear like the laws of nature, if this belief exists in the religion.

The deviation which arose among the People of the Book, which ruined their beliefs and conceptions and their practical life, also began first with the disappearance of true belief in Tawhid. After the disappearance of the belief in Tawhid, other deviations arose.

Most important of all is that the Islamic doctrine of Tawhid has the distinctive quality that it penetrates very deeply into human life. Islam desires that the whole life of human beings be founded on this belief, and that the practical system of human life be entirely established on the foundation of the belief of Tawhid. Just as the effects are in beliefs and conceptions, so too should Shari'ah and law be. And the greatest of such effects, and the greatest of its results, is that human life be governed by the Divine Shari'ah. If these effects do not appear after the affirmation of Tawhid, it will be understood that the belief of Tawhid does not exist, because when the belief of Tawhid of Islam enters the heart, it sprouts in the form of the pillars of life, the system of life, and deeds.

The meaning of Allah being "Ahad" is that He is "Samad," that is, He needs no one, and everyone needs Him. And that He is neither the offspring of anyone nor has He any offspring, and there is none like Him. But after "Ahad," these other meanings have been mentioned separately merely for clarification.

"Allah, the Samad" (112:2): "Allah is free of all needs." The lexical meaning of Samad is one whose command is not settled without His permission. Allah is that Lord besides whom there is no lord and master. He is unique in His divinity, and all are His servants. And He alone is the one who fulfills needs. He is the one who answers the call of every caller, and every matter is decided by His command, and in that decision no one shares with Him. And this meaning is fully present in the word Ahad itself.

"He neither begets nor is He begotten" (112:3). The Being of Allah is a reality which is eternal and everlasting, and His essence cannot change from one state to another. His attribute is that He is absolutely perfect, and in all circumstances the Divine Being is perfect. The process of birth is known to all, consisting of separation and growth. Coming into existence from non-existence, or advancing from deficiency to perfection, are in fact the signs of birth, and Allah is free of these things. Further, birth requires a spouse, and a spouse is always of the same kind as the husband, and this too is impossible for Allah. And within the meaning of God's being Ahad is included that He is neither a father of anyone nor a son.

"And there is none equal to Him" (112:4). He has neither a like nor an equal: neither in the reality of existence, nor in agency, nor in any of His essential or attributive qualities. And this point too is present in the word "Ahad." Since He is Ahad, He has no equal. All these phrases are emphasis and explanation of "Ahad." This belief refutes the Zoroastrian belief that Allah is the god of good and another is the god of evil. This is the self-invented belief of the followers of dualistic beliefs. This belief was prevalent in Iran; accordingly, the Iranians held that there is one god of good and another god of evil, one god of light and another god of darkness, and in the south of the Arabian Peninsula some people held these beliefs, where the Iranians had rule.

This Surah fully establishes the belief of Tawhid of Islam, just as Surah Al-Kafirun has the theme that there can be no compromise or reconciliation between the belief of Tawhid and shirk. Therefore the theme of both Surahs is, from different angles, the belief of Tawhid itself. The Prophet ﷺ used to begin his daily routine with the two Sunnah prayers of Fajr, and in them he would recite these two Surahs. And their recitation in the Fajr Sunnah was purposeful, and this too is evident.

Rather, the demand of the Islamic system is continuous struggle, lasting effort, that humanity be advanced to ever higher levels, and that human life be fully free and liberated. Thus one aspect of worldly life is that it is the office of divine vicegerency, which has its own responsibilities, but in discharging these responsibilities, a person is neither a slave to them nor free of them, as we have explained.

There is one way of escaping the world which the churches prescribed, but Islam does not subscribe to monastic renunciation, because a human being has to perform the duties of earthly vicegerency, and people need good leadership. These two matters are necessary for human salvation, deliverance, and freedom from the slavery of this world. This path is very difficult; that is, the realization of human humanity is possible only in this manner. In this way, spirituality comes to dominate the personality of a human being, and this is freedom: the human soul, freed from worldly defilements, returns freely to its original source, and while working in the world in which Allah has placed a human being after creating him, he maintains his lofty spiritual station and reality.

This is why, at the beginning of the prophetic mission, the call was restricted solely to the belief of Tawhid, and in the above sense an attempt was made to establish the belief of Tawhid in people's minds, because in this sense Tawhid is a belief settled in the human heart and conscience, it is also an interpretation, explanation and understanding of this universe, and it is also a complete system of life. In this meaning, the belief of Tawhid is not merely words which are affirmed by the tongue, nor merely a firm conviction of the human conscience and consciousness which remains hidden only within conscience and consciousness. It is all of this, it is the whole religion; rather, it is the details of this belief. It has certain consequences, and these details and consequences are the natural and necessary results of this belief, and these results appear like the laws of nature, if this belief exists in the religion.

The deviation which arose among the People of the Book, which ruined their beliefs and conceptions and their practical life, also began first with the disappearance of true belief in Tawhid. After the disappearance of the belief in Tawhid, other deviations arose.

Most important of all is that the Islamic doctrine of Tawhid has the distinctive quality that it penetrates very deeply into human life. Islam desires that the whole life of human beings be founded on this belief, and that the practical system of human life be entirely established on the foundation of the belief of Tawhid. Just as the effects are in beliefs and conceptions, so too should Shari'ah and law be. And the greatest of such effects, and the greatest of its results, is that human life be governed by the Divine Shari'ah. If these effects do not appear after the affirmation of Tawhid, it will be understood that the belief of Tawhid does not exist, because when the belief of Tawhid of Islam enters the heart, it sprouts in the form of the pillars of life, the system of life, and deeds.

The meaning of Allah being "Ahad" is that He is "Samad," that is, He needs no one, and everyone needs Him. And that He is neither the offspring of anyone nor has He any offspring, and there is none like Him. But after "Ahad," these other meanings have been mentioned separately merely for clarification.

"Allah, the Samad" (112:2): "Allah is free of all needs." The lexical meaning of Samad is one whose command is not settled without His permission. Allah is that Lord besides whom there is no lord and master. He is unique in His divinity, and all are His servants. And He alone is the one who fulfills needs. He is the one who answers the call of every caller, and every matter is decided by His command, and in that decision no one shares with Him. And this meaning is fully present in the word Ahad itself.

"He neither begets nor is He begotten" (112:3). The Being of Allah is a reality which is eternal and everlasting, and His essence cannot change from one state to another. His attribute is that He is absolutely perfect, and in all circumstances the Divine Being is perfect. The process of birth is known to all, consisting of separation and growth. Coming into existence from non-existence, or advancing from deficiency to perfection, are in fact the signs of birth, and Allah is free of these things. Further, birth requires a spouse, and a spouse is always of the same kind as the husband, and this too is impossible for Allah. And within the meaning of God's being Ahad is included that He is neither a father of anyone nor a son.

"And there is none equal to Him" (112:4). He has neither a like nor an equal: neither in the reality of existence, nor in agency, nor in any of His essential or attributive qualities. And this point too is present in the word "Ahad." Since He is Ahad, He has no equal. All these phrases are emphasis and explanation of "Ahad." This belief refutes the Zoroastrian belief that Allah is the god of good and another is the god of evil. This is the self-invented belief of the followers of dualistic beliefs. This belief was prevalent in Iran; accordingly, the Iranians held that there is one god of good and another god of evil, one god of light and another god of darkness, and in the south of the Arabian Peninsula some people held these beliefs, where the Iranians had rule.

This Surah fully establishes the belief of Tawhid of Islam, just as Surah Al-Kafirun has the theme that there can be no compromise or reconciliation between the belief of Tawhid and shirk. Therefore the theme of both Surahs is, from different angles, the belief of Tawhid itself. The Prophet ﷺ used to begin his daily routine with the two Sunnah prayers of Fajr, and in them he would recite these two Surahs. And their recitation in the Fajr Sunnah was purposeful, and this too is evident.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 112, verses 1–4:

Say, "He is Allah, the One" (112:1). The word "Ahad" is deeper than "Wahid," because Ahad adds to the meaning of Wahid that nothing else truly exists alongside Him, and there is nothing like Him; that is, He is unique.

In "Ahad" there is an expression of the oneness of existence (wujud): that is, there is no reality other than His reality, and there is no true existence other than His. All existent things other than Allah derive their existence from Allah and take their reality from His reality. He is also One in agency (fa'iliyyah), so in this whole universe there is no other effective cause and no other agent besides Allah. Therefore, this is a doctrine and belief that settles in the conscience of a human being, and it is in fact also the interpretation of this universe. When this belief takes root in a heart, and reason conceives of it, and the whole universe is interpreted in its light, then no other conception overshadows the human heart, and no other thought remains even a trace in the human heart. The human heart then has no connection with anyone except that One Being, the Necessary Existent, because in truth the One Being alone truly exists, and it is this One Being alone who acts and causes effect.

Then the connection of the human heart with all the things found in this universe comes to an end. Although the ideal would be that awareness of the existence of anything other than Allah itself disappears from the human heart, even if this awareness does not disappear, the connection ends, because apart from the existence of Allah, the existence of all other things has no reality. And in this whole universe, nothing other than the agency and influence of Allah's will is active and effective. So why should the heart of one who holds the belief of Tawhid be attached to something that neither truly exists nor is active and effective in anything?

Now, when the heart becomes empty of the conception of the reality of all things other than the One God, and has no connection with anything other than Allah, then this heart truly becomes free; it becomes free of every kind of restriction. All its desires end, and the truth is that desires are in fact the chains on the feet. Then fear also departs from this heart, and it should be remembered that a person is also bound in chains because of fear. Why do the enjoyable things of the world end in the heart of a person? Because when he attains Allah, he attains everything, and he does not fear because he comes to know that there is no effective agent other than Allah.

When the reality settles firmly in human consciousness that in this universe a person sees only the reality of Allah, the result is that whatever existence he then sees in this universe, he will see the same reality in it. In this way, the human heart sees the hand of power (dast-e-qudrat) in everything, and after this, a person reaches the rank where he sees nothing in this universe except Allah.

As a result of this belief and conception, a person begins to think that apparent causes are also insignificant. The real and true cause is the Causer of causes, that is, the Divine Being. This is the point to which the Qur'an has given much attention, and it has sought to place it in the minds of people by making it part of the articles of faith of Islam. Accordingly, by setting aside apparent causes, it has been explained that the real cause is the Divine Will.

"And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw" (8:17). And in Al-Imran (3:126) it was said: "Victory is only from Allah." And in Al-Insan (76:30): "And you do not will except that Allah wills." There are countless verses of this kind.

When a person sets aside apparent causes, then he sees that all matters are determined by the will of Allah. From this, tranquility arises in his heart; now he seeks all desirable things from Allah and seeks refuge with Allah to protect himself from all undesirable things, and the apparent factors, apparent causes and influences which appear to act in this universe have no reality in his eyes.

These are the stations which the Sufis have sought to traverse. But the attraction of these stations took them far away. The Sufis could not understand that Islam, by calling people, certainly takes them to these lofty stations, but it takes them there while keeping them within all the ups and downs of practical worldly life, within every kind of human life, and while performing the duties of vicegerency (niyabat) of Allah on this earth. They participate fully in the life of this world and also consider it insignificant. They live in this universe, but they regard only Allah as the truly existent. They regard Allah as the one who is active and effective in all events and occurrences. And Islam adopts no other method than this, nor does it desire any other. As a result, a complete system of life comes into being. This system has come into being as a result of this interpretation of the universe and the consciousness, conceptions and tendencies arising from it. What are the features of this system of life?

(1) This system has its own system of worship in which only Allah is worshipped, the Allah whose existence has no reality apart from His existence, whose agency has no other agency besides it, and no other will is effective besides His will.

(2) This is a system in which a person turns in every state, in hope and in fear, only to Allah. In joy and in sorrow, in wealth and in poverty, in short, in every state his direction is only towards Allah alone. This is because in this system every person knows that when no other thing has real existence apart from Allah, then what is the benefit of turning to or calling upon it? When there is no agent or effective cause other than Allah, then what would be gained by turning towards anything else?

(3) This is a system in which guidance is taken only from Allah. Beliefs and doctrines, values and standards, Shari'ah and law, institutions and administration, customs and traditions, manners and conventions, all are derived from Allah. Therefore, every kind of guidance and direction is taken only from Allah alone, who is the One Existent both in reality and in the conscience of a Muslim.

(4) This system is a system of movement and action, and this movement and action is solely for Allah alone: for seeking His pleasure, for seeking His nearness, in the hope that on the path to reaching Him all veils and obstacles will be removed, and a person will be protected from all the impurities of misguidance, whether these veils and obstacles are within the human self, or come from the things and people of the human environment, among which the self of a person, the fear of people, his desires, and the things he loves in this world are foremost.

(5) This is a system which, alongside the above matters, creates a relationship of love, affection, cooperation and harmony between the human heart and all the existents of this universe. This is because freedom from the bonds of the world does not mean that a person regards it as detestable, hates it, flees from it, and refrains from using it. This is because all the things of the world are the wonders of Allah's power. Their existence is derived from the existence of Allah, and upon all things the light of that reality falls. Therefore all these things are beloved, because they are gifts of Allah, who is the Beloved.
